## Summary

For all their apparent simplicity, maps make evocative statements about the way the world is – embellished, as they are with textual detail, colours, shading and the like. The maps of Africa that European merchants and explorers generated in previous centuries are so captivating to modern eyes precisely because they obviously distort size and shape – and famously fill in the empty spaces in inventive ways.1 Contemporary cartography is less obviously idiosyncratic, but it harbours its own blind spots and pointed omissions – which becomes painfully obvious when actors are first confronted with the puzzling unfamiliarity of a map depicting a place they know intimately. As others have noted, maps are not innocent things, but have historically been associated with projects of state-making and enclosure in different parts of the world – including those bound up with empire.2 The seductive power of maps resides in their normalizing character, which serves to close down alternative ways of seeing while authorizing particular modes of doing. In that sense, maps have been constitutive of power relations in their own right.

## ABSTRACT

How have colonial captivity systems been remembered and mis-remembered in the U.S. Borderlands? I approach the history of female captivity in New Spain through two intertwining lenses: nineteenth- and twentieth-century representations of captivity, which often flatten or erase female agency, and female-equine relations found in the Borderlands colonial archive and in oral histories. Los Comanches, an eighteenth-century play performed until recent years on horseback in New Mexico, contains complex allusions to captivity history yet includes no women, in reference or in body. Examining the roles of equine actors in the play led me to instances of female-equine interaction in the captivity archive and glimpses of female pain, agency, and knowledge. Through a textured annotation of Los Comanches, this paper inserts women’s stories and sensory experiences into collective memories of captivity history. Asserting the value of telling history through a poetic form, I give body to the outlined traces of women in the colonial archive while leaving visible the record’s violences and the impossibility of fully restoring the past. ## History and historiography

In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, Comanche, Apache, Ute, Diné, and Pueblo members and leaders, Genízaro soldiers and families, Spanish settlers, and New Mexican traders and civilians created an elaborate system of trading goods and captives.Footnote^{10} Historians have approached this system with varying degrees of sensitivity to agency and power structures.Footnote^{11} None have dwelled on the relationship between horses and women in captivity logics or commemoration.Footnote^{12} Abundant scholarship exists on networks of power in the Borderlands, the relationships between Apaches, Utes, Diné, Pueblo peoples, and Comanches, and the extent of the Comanches’ imperial power in the region. Many works debate the various motivations of captive-taking across the colonial period: increasing population in the face of decline, growing cattle and equine stock, and supplementing labor in a period of colonial expansion and ecological violence (Brooks Citation2002; Hämäläinen Citation2010; Rivaya-Martínez Citation2014a). --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Book description

Border regions are often considered to be the neglected margins. In this book, Paul Nugent argues that through a comparison of the Senegambia and the trans-Volta (Ghana/Togo), we can see that the geographical margins have shaped notional centres at least as much as the reverse. Through a study of three centuries of history, this book demonstrates that states were forged through an extended process of converting a topography of settled states and slaving frontiers into colonial borders. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
